loText: Differentiate between through-the-cycle credit rating system and point-in-time credit rating system.
question: A quantitative model validator at a credit rating agency in country WYZ is reviewing models developed by a credit risk analytics group. The validator observes that the rating migration matrix model is based on the data from 2013 to 2022. During these 10 years the economy of country WYZ experienced a mild recession as well as periods of economic growth. However, it is expected that in 2023 a severe downturn greater in magnitude than any previously observed downturn will hit the economy. Which of the following observations would the validator be correct to make?

options.A: The rating migration matrix uses the through-the-cycle approach to managing data and will underestimate the default probabilities for the year 2023.
options.B: The rating migration matrix uses the through-the-cycle approach to managing data and will overestimate the default probabilities for the year 2023.
options.C: The rating migration matrix uses the point-in-time approach to managing data and will underestimate the default probabilities for the year 2023.
options.D: The rating migration matrix uses the point-in-time approach to managing data and will overestimate the default probabilities for the year 2023.

solution:
**Concept**

A through-the-cycle rating or migration matrix averages over a full economic cycle, so it is stable but slow to reflect current conditions. A point-in-time measure reflects the conditions of the moment. An average over good and mildly bad years understates defaults in a severe downturn and overstates them in a boom.

**Exam trap.** Two decisions in one option: the label (through-the-cycle versus point-in-time) and the direction of the error. Settle each separately. The average of mild years is always too optimistic for a severe year.

loText: Discuss the “dark side” of retail credit risk and the measures that attempt to address the problem.
question: A credit manager at a US-based commercial bank asks a team of risk analysts to examine the risks attributed to a large retail credit portfolio of the bank. The manager instructs the analyst to suggest measures to mitigate the “dark side” of retail credit risk affecting the portfolio. Which of the following would most likely be an effective measure?

options.A: Focus the extension of credit on low default portfolios such as mortgages or large corporations.
options.B: Concentrate on expected loss estimation since systematic risk factors such as a real estate crisis or a sharp economic downturn can be diversified away.
options.C: Monitor the effectiveness of credit risk assessment tools for retail customers and adjust the tools as needed.
options.D: Use stress tests to analyze the exposure to idiosyncratic risk factors of every single retail credit customer.

solution:
**Concept**

Retail portfolios look safe because they are granular, so expected loss dominates. The “dark side” is a sudden jump in losses when a systematic factor (house prices, a downturn, a flawed or untested scoring tool) hits many customers at once.

**Exam trap.** Systematic factors cannot be diversified away, however many small loans there are. Stress tests measure the risk; they do not mitigate it.
